new_d.text: Deleuze's project in Difference and Repetition (1968): a concept of difference that comes before identity and explains how identities are produced, freed from its subordination to representation.

new_text.text: Difference and Repetition was Deleuze's principal thesis for the Doctorat d'État (Paul Patton, Translator's Preface).
Its first chapter opens with lightning, which distinguishes itself from a black sky that does not distinguish itself from it: difference as a one-sided distinction (p. 28).
Identity, for Deleuze, is a second principle, produced by what differs (pp. 40–41).
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).
Representation subordinates difference to identity in the concept, opposition between predicates, analogy in judgement and resemblance in perception (pp. 29, 34; see Representation).
In Aristotle's division of a genus by specific differences, Deleuze's example is animals with feet and animals with wings (p. 30): difference counts only inside an identical concept.

Deleuze rejects Hegel's contradiction, which in his reading is the greatest difference only in relation to the identical (pp. 49–52, 263), and against Plato's models and copies he sets the simulacrum, calling for an overturning of Platonism that Plato himself, he argues, was the first to point toward (pp. 59–69).
The third chapter lists eight postulates of the dogmatic image of thought, among them the good nature of thought, common sense and recognition (p. 167).

Thought begins, on Deleuze's account, with an encounter with something that forces it to think (pp. 139–145); he takes Kant's sublime as the case in which the faculties work in discord (p. 146), and he gives learning, the encounter with a problem, the place that knowledge held in the dogmatic image (pp. 164–167).

Repetition, Deleuze argues, belongs to another order from generality, which is the order of laws (pp. 1–3), and he calls it difference without a concept (pp. 13, 23), a formula the rest of the Introduction fills out with internal difference and the Idea (pp. 24–27).
Repetition for itself, following his reading of the eternal return, is the return of what differs (pp. 41, 90–94).
Chapter 5 opens by calling difference “that by which the given is given” (p. 222), and sets it apart from diversity, which is what is given.

Differences of temperature, pressure and potential are among its examples (p. 222); an intensive quantity “may be divided, but not without changing its nature” (p. 237); and individuation precedes the differenciation of species and parts in principle (pp. 246–250).
The Stanford Encyclopedia article's example of a process driven by intensive differences is convection.
Guides include Joe Hughes's Deleuze's Difference and Repetition: A Reader's Guide (2009), James Williams's critical introduction and guide (2003) and Henry Somers-Hall's Edinburgh guide (2013).

new_d.text: The three syntheses of time in chapter 2 of Difference and Repetition: habit, which founds the living present; memory, which grounds its passing in the pure past; and the empty form of time, in whose third time Deleuze places the eternal return.

new_text.text: The second chapter of Difference and Repetition, “Repetition for Itself”, sets out three passive syntheses of time, which, Deleuze writes, “must be understood as constitutive of the unconscious” (p. 114).
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).

The first starts from Hume's thesis that repetition changes nothing in the object repeated and something in the mind that contemplates it, and contracts successive instants into a living present (pp. 70–71).
The synthesis is passive: it “occurs in the mind which contemplates, prior to all memory and all reflection” (p. 71).
Its contractions are the work of contemplative souls (pp. 73–76), and “Selves are larval subjects” (p. 78).
Habit is the foundation of time, and memory its ground (p. 79).

The second synthesis is the pure past, which Deleuze develops from Bergson's paradoxes: the past is contemporaneous with the present it was, the whole past coexists with each present, and it pre-exists the passing present (pp. 81–83).
Memory's active reproduction of former presents rests on “another (transcendental) passive synthesis” peculiar to memory itself (p. 81).
Deleuze pairs it with Eros and Mnemosyne, and his example is Proust's Combray, which reappears “in the form of a past which was never present” (p. 85).
The third synthesis is the pure and empty form of time, in which time is “out of joint” (pp. 88–89): a caesura orders it into a before and an after, and the I is fractured.

Deleuze distinguishes the order, the totality and the series of time, and places the eternal return in the third time of the series alone, the future, which brings back neither the condition nor the agent (pp. 88–90).

The Stanford Encyclopedia article describes the syntheses of habit as bodily, desiring and unconscious contractions, and subjects as patterns of syntheses that fold in on themselves, producing “a site of self-awareness”.

In the same chapter Deleuze turns to Freud: binding excitations makes possible “the value taken on by pleasure as a principle” (p. 96), and in his revision of Freud, Thanatos is “completely indistinguishable from the desexualisation of Eros” (p. 113).

Joe Hughes reads the three syntheses as a genesis running from sensibility toward thought (Hughes, pp. 86–88), and notes that James Williams and many others read the third as operating before the first (Hughes, p. 78).
Williams has also written Gilles Deleuze's Philosophy of Time (2011), which has not been read for this entry.

new_d.text: Deleuze's distinction, which he credits to Bergson, between the virtual, the real structure of a thing as an Idea of differential relations and singularities, and the actual qualities and parts in which that structure is embodied.

new_text.text: “The virtual is fully real in so far as it is virtual”, Deleuze writes, and it must be defined as “strictly a part of the real object” (pp. 208–209): every object has a virtual part and an actual part.
He separates the virtual from the possible: the possible is realized, and the real is supposed to resemble it, while the virtual is actualized by difference, divergence and creation (pp. 211–212).

In a note he names Bergson as the author who “pushes furthest the critique of the possible” (ch. 4, n. 23, p. 327), and the Stanford Encyclopedia article notes that he had developed virtuality and multiplicity in Bergsonism (1966).
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).
An Idea, Deleuze's name for a virtual structure, is “an n-dimensional, continuous, defined multiplicity” (p. 182).

Three conditions define it: elements with neither sensible form nor conceptual signification, reciprocal relations that determine them, and the actualization of such a relation in diverse spatio-temporal relationships, its elements incarnated in a variety of terms and forms (p. 183).
Multiplicity, the Stanford article explains, designates the multiple as a substantive.
The differential elements of a language are its phonemes, and Deleuze asks why Saussure calls linguistic differences negative and why Trubetzkoy makes difference presuppose opposition (pp. 203–205).

Deleuze distinguishes differentiation, the determination of the Idea's virtual content, from differenciation, its actualization in species and qualities and in distinct parts and extensities, and joins them as different/ciation (pp. 207, 209–211).

Between the two lies intensity: individuation is intensive, Gilbert Simondon has shown that it presupposes a prior metastable state, and individuation precedes differenciation in principle (pp. 246–247).
The Stanford article takes Simondon's supersaturated solution, metastable before it crystallizes, as a simple model.
Deleuze's later work with Guattari, and readers after them, take the distinction into other books.
In the Stanford article's account of Deleuze and Guattari's A Thousand Plateaus, the virtual is called the Earth, the intensive consistency and the actual the system of the strata.
The article names Brian Massumi and Manuel DeLanda, author of Intensive Science and Virtual Philosophy (2002), among those who bring Deleuze's ontology together with dynamical systems theory.

new_d.text: The thesis that being is said in one and the same sense of everything of which it is said; in Difference and Repetition Deleuze reconstructs its history through Duns Scotus, Spinoza and Nietzsche and makes it the basis of a philosophy of difference.

new_text.text: Medieval philosophers debated how terms apply to God and to creatures: Thomas Aquinas held that we can predicate only analogically, and John Duns Scotus that certain predicates apply univocally, with exactly the same meaning, to both.
Since all our concepts come from creatures, Scotus argued, without univocity we could not talk about God at all.
“There has only ever been one ontological proposition: Being is univocal”, Deleuze declares (p. 35).
Being is “said in a single and same sense of everything of which it is said”, and what it is said of differs: it is said of difference itself (p. 36).

What matters in univocity, he writes, is that being is said in that one sense “of all its individuating differences or intrinsic modalities” (p. 36), and the Stanford Encyclopedia article calls univocity the key to a philosophy of difference.
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).

Univocal being keeps a hierarchy of its own beside the equality of being: one that considers beings “from the point of view of power”, asking whether a being goes to the limit of what it can do (p. 37).
It also demands that individuating difference come before generic and specific differences (p. 38).
Deleuze tells its history in three moments (pp. 39–41).
Scotus thought univocal being and neutralized it in an abstract concept.
Spinoza made it an object of pure affirmation, identified with a single substance, and from his account follows “a determination of modes as degrees of power” (p. 40).

Spinoza's substance still appears independent of the modes, and Deleuze demands a reversal, “Substance must itself be said of the modes and only of the modes” (p. 40), which Nietzsche's eternal return carries out, making identity “a secondary power” (p. 41).

Deleuze's secondary thesis was Expressionism in Philosophy: Spinoza (1968) (Patton, Translator's Preface), and the Stanford article describes the result of his reading as “a Spinozism minus substance, a purely modal or differential universe”.
The article defines puissance as immanent power, the power to act, and links pouvoir to transcendent power.

Joe Hughes follows Deleuze's account of degrees of power, which he quotes from a 1974 seminar, and then asks whether univocity really reduces everything to equal participation in being and a capacity to be affected; he stresses that univocal being is said of a pre-individual world of individuating factors (Hughes, pp. 57–59).
Celeste Ramírez reads univocity against the vertical, transcendent hierarchy of genera and species.

Alain Badiou's Deleuze: The Clamor of Being (1997) argued, as the Stanford article reports, that Deleuze is at bottom a philosopher of the One, and criticized his vitalism; this entry leaves that dispute open.

new_d.text: Deleuze's name, in Difference and Repetition (1968), for the way of thinking that makes difference intelligible only by relating it to identity: identity in the concept, opposition in the predicate, analogy in judgement and resemblance in perception.

new_text.text: Deleuze calls these four forms “the four shackles of mediation” (p. 29), and in the Conclusion “the four iron collars of representation” (p. 262).

In chapter 3 he lists them again, “identity with regard to concepts”, “opposition with regard to the determination of concepts”, “analogy with regard to judgement” and “resemblance with regard to objects”, and ties them to recognition, the form of the Same (pp. 137–138).
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).

In Deleuze's reading of Aristotle, specific difference divides a genus into species, as animals with feet and animals with wings divide the genus animal (p. 30), so difference counts only inside an identical concept.

The large genera are related by analogy in judgement and the small units, the species, by a perception of resemblances (p. 34), while individual difference is too small to count (pp. 30–31); univocal being, Deleuze argues, demands that individuating difference precede generic, specific and even individual differences (p. 38).

Leibniz and Hegel, he argues, carry representation into the infinite and make it orgiastic: Leibniz through vice-diction and a technique for the infinitely small, Hegel through contradiction and a technique for the infinitely large (pp. 42–52, 262–263).
Both still keep identity in charge, on his account: infinite representation stays bound to the convergence of series in Leibniz and to the monocentring of circles in Hegel (p. 49).

Joe Hughes's Reader's Guide (2009) takes representation to be the object, with its qualities and its extension, and reads Deleuze's critique as radical in the sense that it must show how what it criticizes was produced (Hughes, pp. 1–3).

Hughes traces Deleuze's engagement with Hegel largely to Jean Hyppolite, who read the Phenomenology of Spirit as the genetic development of consciousness through determinate negation, and he sets this against Deleuze's claim that contradiction is less profound than difference (Hughes, pp. 46–50); Hyppolite's own books have not been read for this entry.

Deleuze's alternative runs through univocity, in which being is said of individuating differences (pp. 35–42); the eternal return, in which identity becomes “a secondary power” (p. 41); the simulacrum, with which Plato, on Deleuze's reading, was the first to show the direction in which Platonism could be overturned (pp. 59–69); and the Ideas of chapter 4, whose differential relations are actualized in qualities and parts (pp. 182–184, 207–212).

new_d.text: Deleuze's term, in Difference and Repetition (1968), for the recurrence of what is singular and cannot be replaced, set against generality, in which one particular can be exchanged for another.

new_text.text: The book opens by separating repetition from generality: generality belongs to the order of laws and to exchange or substitution, where one particular can take another's place, and repetition concerns singularities that cannot be exchanged (pp. 1–3).
Festivals, Deleuze writes, “repeat an ‘unrepeatable’” (p. 1).
Pages of Difference and Repetition are from Paul Patton's translation (1994).
He calls repetition “difference without a concept” (pp. 13, 23) and distinguishes two forms (pp. 23–25).

Bare repetition is the repetition of the same, occurrences that differ only externally, under one identical concept; covered or clothed repetition forms itself “in masking and disguising itself” (p. 24).
The two depend on each other: the clothed is “the singular subject” of the bare, and the bare is “only the external envelope” (p. 24).

In chapter 2 repetition takes three forms in time: habit contracts instants into a living present (pp. 70–79), memory grounds the passing present in a pure past whose levels coexist virtually (pp. 79–85), and the third synthesis is the empty form of time, ordered by a caesura into a before and an after (pp. 88–90).
The eternal return, Deleuze writes, concerns “only the third time of the series” (p. 90), the future, and brings back neither the condition nor the agent.
With it, “repetition is, for itself, difference in itself” (p. 94).
The Conclusion sets the bare, the clothed and the repetition of the eternal return side by side, and reads Nietzsche's Zarathustra as a drama of a selective return (pp. 296–300).
Joe Hughes reads repetition as what explains representation (Hughes, p. 27) and the three syntheses as a genesis running from sensibility toward thought (Hughes, pp. 86–88).

On his reading the third synthesis is a failed synthesis of recognition, in which the cogito becomes what Deleuze, after Paul Ricoeur, calls an “aborted cogito” (p. 110), and the eternal return appears only in the third time, after it (Hughes, pp. 115–116, 124–125).

Hughes notes in one sentence that James Williams and many others read the third synthesis as operating before the first, and argues for the order Deleuze gives (Hughes, p. 78); Williams's own books have not been read for this entry.

Deleuze speaks of “virtual coexistence between the levels of a pure past” (p. 83); Hughes argues that the virtual of chapter 4 appears only after the third synthesis, so the pure past should not be equated with it (Hughes, pp. 111–112), and this entry leaves that question open.

summary: Six entries on Difference and Repetition checked against the book: two new (representation, repetition) and four re-read. Every quotation is verbatim; the book corrected the earlier, encyclopedia-based text in several places (Deleuze's own example of specific difference, the IEP's 'active' second synthesis, Bergson's credit, the secondary thesis's English title), and Hughes's disagreements with the text are given as open disputes.
